title: Dynamic programming
summary: Solve a big problem by building it up from the answers to smaller versions of the same problem, each worked out only once.

sections.heading: The idea
body: Dynamic programming fits when an answer can be built from answers to smaller versions of the same question, and those smaller questions repeat.
There are two ways to write it:
- **Top down**: plain recursion plus a memo, as in the Recursion note.
- **Bottom up**: fill a table from the smallest case upwards. No recursion, so no stack limits.
The hard part is finding the rule that links an answer to smaller ones. Say it in words first: "the number of ways to reach step `i` is the ways to reach `i - 1` plus the ways to reach `i - 2`".

sections.heading: Bottom up: climbing stairs
body: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many different ways are there to reach step `n`? The last move came from step `n - 1` or from step `n - 2`, so add those two answers.

sections.heading: When the obvious greedy choice is wrong
body: Fewest coins to make an amount: grabbing the biggest coin first works for everyday coins, but not always. With coins 1, 3 and 4, greedy makes 6 as 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins); the best is 3 + 3 (two).
The table version tries every coin for every amount from 1 upwards: the best for `total` is one coin plus the best for `total - coin`.

sections.heading: Two dimensions: comparing two strings
body: Some problems need a grid. The longest common subsequence of two words (letters in the same order, not necessarily next to each other) uses `table[i][j]` = the answer for the first `i` letters of one word and the first `j` of the other.
If the letters match, take the diagonal answer plus one; otherwise take the better of the cell above and the cell to the left.

mistakes: Forgetting the starting values (the base cases) of the table.
Making the table one too small: amounts and lengths usually need `n + 1` slots so that 0 fits.
Assuming the greedy choice is optimal without checking a small counter-example.
